subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: Last week our teacher asked me what a noun is, and I said, “Hmm… uh… a noun is… um…” Some kids giggled. My hands went cold. I thought they believed I didn't know. But I did know, I just needed a moment to pick the right words. Miss waited, and I said, “A noun is the name of a person, place or thing.” She smiled and nodded. Later I told Aparna I say hmm when my brain is looking through its drawers. She said hers does too. Now I don't mind so much when the sounds slip out. I'm Rukmini and I like thinking time.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask Rukmini?
qa.a: What a noun is.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel when some kids giggled at the hmm and um?
qa.a: Rukmini felt nervous, with cold hands and the worry that the class thought the answer was unknown. In fact Rukmini knew it and just needed a moment to pick the words.

qa.q: What could a teacher do to help a child who uses these sounds?
qa.a: She could wait a few seconds, like Miss did, so the child can finish the thought.

qa.q: How might the giggling classmates have seen Rukmini's hmm and um?
qa.a: They may have taken the sounds as not knowing, which is one way to read them, though the correct answer shows otherwise.

grounding: A schoolchild uses hmm, uh and um while thinking, and a teacher who waits gets a good answer.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: Observation note, Class 4. Sarika was asked to explain why ice melts. She said, “Uh... hmm... it's because... um,” and looked at the window. Two classmates put up their hands. Usually I would have called on one of them within a moment. This time I counted silently and kept my eyes friendly. After what felt like a long while, Sarika said, “Because it gets warm and the water inside can move.” It was a thoughtful answer. I asked her what she had been doing in her head. She said, “Looking for how to say it.” I plan to wait longer with all pupils. Ms. Lavanya.

qa.q: What was Sarika asked to explain?
qa.a: Why ice melts.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt while saying hmm and um?
qa.a: She probably felt unsure and under pressure while searching for words, and she told the teacher she was looking for how to say it.

qa.q: What did the teacher change that helped, and what might she try next?
qa.a: Lavanya waited quietly instead of switching to another pupil, and she plans to wait longer with all pupils.

qa.q: How might the two classmates with their hands up have felt while waiting?
qa.a: They may have felt impatient because they knew their answers, but a short wait taught them that a thoughtful answer can arrive slowly.

grounding: Fillers like hmm, uh and um show the mind at work, and a teacher who waits gets a better answer.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: Friday. Naveen's diary. In the social science oral today, Damini Ma'am asked me why rivers are important for farming. I knew it, but my mouth said, “Umm… uh… hmm.” Last year Sir always said, “Next!” the second I said umm, and I'd go red. Today Damini Ma'am just waited. She looked out of the window like she had all day. The umms went on for a bit, and then my brain caught up: water for the fields, soil from the floods, and villages growing up beside them. She nodded and wrote something down. At the end she said, “Your umm means you're thinking. Keep thinking.” I got nine out of ten.

qa.q: What did Damini Ma'am ask Naveen?
qa.a: She asked why rivers are important for farming.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while saying “umm” at first?
qa.a: Naveen felt nervous, remembering being cut off with “Next!” last year, even though the answer was there.

qa.q: Why did Damini Ma'am's waiting work?
qa.a: Waiting gave Naveen's thinking time to catch up, so the umms led to a full, correct answer.

qa.q: How did last year's Sir seem to read the umms?
qa.a: Last year's Sir seemed to read them as not knowing, cutting Naveen off instead of waiting.

grounding: Shows a child's umms and hmms as thinking sounds, and a teacher who waits getting a better answer.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: At the village library under the peepal tree, Santosh Sir asked the children what the story's ending meant. Asif put up his hand, then said, “Hmm… uh… um.” Two older boys sniggered. “He doesn't know.” Santosh Sir held up one finger to them and turned back to Asif, waiting. The breeze rattled the leaves. A cow lowed somewhere. Asif's eyes were moving, as if reading something inside his head. “Um… the crow didn't really want the cheese,” he said slowly. “It wanted the fox to see it was clever.” Santosh Sir's eyebrows went up. “Nobody's ever said that. Tell me more.”

qa.q: Where was the village library?
qa.a: The village library was under the peepal tree.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling while he hummed and paused?
qa.a: Asif was thinking hard and a bit unsure, working out a new idea, not showing that he didn't know.

qa.q: How did Santosh Sir make space for Asif's answer?
qa.a: He silenced the sniggering boys with a finger and waited, which let Asif finish a thoughtful new idea.

qa.q: How did the older boys read Asif's thinking sounds?
qa.a: They took the umms as a sign he didn't know the answer.

grounding: Shows a child's hmm, uh and um as the mind at work, and a teacher who waits hearing a fresh answer.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: Diego had been in Copenhagen for three months, and in maths his English still came out slowly. When Mr Lars Holm asked him to explain how he'd found the answer, Diego said, “Ehh… este… um.” A girl at the next table started to answer for him. Mr Holm raised a hand gently. “Let's give Diego a moment.” Diego stared at his page, lips moving. “Um… I made the big number into tens first. Then… hmm… I added the small ones after.” He looked up. “Is that right?” “It's more than right,” said Mr Holm. “It's a smart way. Show the class.”

qa.q: How long had Diego been in Copenhagen?
qa.a: Diego had been in Copenhagen for three months.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling as he said “Ehh… este… um”?
qa.a: Diego was concentrating and a little unsure, searching for both the method and the English words.

qa.q: Why did Mr Holm stop the girl answering for Diego?
qa.a: Waiting showed that Diego's fillers meant thinking, and it let him share a smart method in his own words.

qa.q: What might the girl at the next table have thought?
qa.a: She probably thought she was helping, reading Diego's pauses as being stuck.

grounding: Shows a child's filler sounds as thinking rather than not knowing, and a teacher who waits getting a better answer.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage:
"Why do you think the leaves on this plant turned yellow, Nitin?" Pema Ma'am held up the sad-looking pot from the window ledge.

"Umm…" Nitin scratched his chin. "Uh… hmm."

Last week, when the substitute teacher asked him something, he'd said "Um" and she'd snapped, "Don't know? Next!" He'd had the answer ten seconds later, too late.

Pema Ma'am just waited, pot in hand. The class shuffled. Nitin looked at the window. "Hmm… it's on the ledge where the sun doesn't come after lunch. And the soil's always wet. Maybe too much water and not enough light?"

Pema Ma'am smiled. "That's two good ideas. Let's test both."

qa.q: Where was the plant pot kept?
qa.a: On the window ledge, where the sun doesn't come after lunch.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling during his "umm" and "hmm"?
qa.a: He was unsure and thinking hard, working the idea out; he may also have felt nervous, remembering last week's snapped "Next!".

qa.q: Which choice brought out Nitin's answer?
qa.a: Pema Ma'am waited quietly instead of moving on, giving him the few seconds he needed 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Pema Ma'am had said "Don't know? Next!" like the substitute?
qa.a: Nitin's two good ideas would have been lost, and he might feel stupid and stop trying to answer.

grounding: It shows a child's hmm and um as signs of thinking, and a teacher who waits getting a better answer than one who rushes.
